title: The Two Diabetes Drugs Most Indians Take May Double the Risk of a Heart Attack. A 132,000-Patient Study Just Proved It.
excerpt: Sulfonylureas and basal insulin are cheap and everywhere. A new JAMA study says they come at a hidden cardiovascular cost that South Asians can least afford.
body:
More than 500 million people worldwide live with type 2 diabetes, and most depend on medication to keep their blood sugar under control. But a new study from Northwestern University has found that two of the most widely prescribed second-line treatments — sulfonylureas and basal insulin — may significantly raise the risk of heart attacks, strokes and heart failure compared with newer alternatives.

The study, published in JAMA Network Open, analysed real-world medical data from more than 132,000 adults with type 2 diabetes who had already been taking metformin and needed an additional medication.

The results were striking. Patients on sulfonylureas had a 36 per cent higher risk of experiencing a major cardiovascular event — heart attacks, strokes or heart failure — compared with those on DPP-4 inhibitors, a newer class of diabetes medication. For patients taking basal insulin, the risk was roughly double.

The practical impact of those numbers is significant. Among patients on basal insulin, one major cardiovascular event occurred for every 37 people treated over a two-year period. For sulfonylureas, the rate was one event per 103 patients in the same window.

"The ideal diabetes medication should not only lower blood sugar but also help protect the heart," said Dr Matthew O'Brien, the study's lead author. He believes the findings should encourage both doctors and patients to look beyond blood sugar control when choosing a treatment.

## Why This Matters for South Asians

The findings carry particular weight for the South Asian diaspora. Indians and their descendants have among the highest rates of type 2 diabetes in the world — roughly one in six Indian adults lives with the condition, and prevalence among South Asians in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada is two to four times higher than in general populations.

What makes this doubly concerning is that sulfonylureas and basal insulin remain the dominant second-line treatments in India and across much of South Asia, largely because they are cheap. A month's supply of glipizide or glimepiride — both sulfonylureas — costs under 100 rupees in many Indian pharmacies. Newer medications such as DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors can cost ten to twenty times as much.

That cost gap means millions of South Asian patients — including the parents and relatives of NRIs who manage medication decisions remotely — may be on treatments that are quietly increasing their cardiovascular risk.

## What the Newer Drugs Offer

Over the past decade, several newer diabetes drug classes have shown the ability to not only manage blood sugar but actively protect the heart. GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and SGLT-2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin have demonstrated reductions in heart failure, stroke and cardiovascular death in large clinical trials.

DPP-4 inhibitors, which served as the comparator in the Northwestern study, occupy a middle ground — they are cardiovascular-neutral, meaning they neither raise nor lower heart risk, but they do not carry the elevated danger seen with older drugs.

The researchers argue that the higher upfront cost of newer medications may be offset by long-term savings from preventing expensive medical emergencies — heart attacks, hospitalisations and heart failure treatment.

## What NRIs Should Know

For diaspora families managing a parent's diabetes care from thousands of miles away, the findings raise an urgent practical question: is your family member still on an older drug when a safer option exists?

The researchers caution that no patient should stop medication without consulting their doctor. But they are clear that the conversation about switching should be happening more often, especially in populations where heart disease is already the leading cause of death.

India's healthcare system is beginning to grapple with this trade-off. The government's Jan Aushadhi programme has started stocking some newer diabetes drugs at subsidised prices, and several Indian pharmaceutical companies are manufacturing generic DPP-4 inhibitors at a fraction of global costs. Whether access catches up with the evidence will determine outcomes for millions.

*Sources: JAMA Network Open (2026); Northwestern University; WHO Diabetes Fact Sheet*
